proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(C=(h,g)\in\mathcal X_{m,K}\) and put \(r=h+g\).  By the two arm-size equalities in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}profile\text{-}space}\),
\[
 \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}r_a
 =\sum_a h_a+\sum_a g_a=2m=n.
\]
Thus \(D_r\) has mass \(n\), as required by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}table\text{-}mass}\).  Every occupied cell of \(D_r\) is diagonal, so
\[
 \sum_{a,b}(a-b)(D_r)_{ab}=0,
\]
which is Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\).  Hence \(D_r\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) by Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}legal\text{-}response\text{-}tables}\).

If \(T\in\mathcal T_{D_r}(C)\), all its off-diagonal entries vanish because \(0\leq T_{ab}\leq(D_r)_{ab}=0\) when \(a\ne b\).  Its row constraints then force \(T_{aa}=h_a\), and its control-column constraints say \(r_a-T_{aa}=g_a\).  The latter equalities hold because \(r=h+g\).  Thus there is exactly one realizing treated-count table and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) gives
\[
 W_{D_r}(C)=\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\binom{r_a}{h_a}=Q_r(h),
\]
where the last equality is Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}diagonal\text{-}coefficient}\).  Each factor is positive because \(0\leq h_a\leq r_a\), so this count is positive.

Finally, under a diagonal response table every unit displays the same alphabet value in either arm.  Hence the pooled observed histogram is deterministically \(r\).  Equivalently, summing the row and control-column constraints for any realizing \(T\) gives \(\widetilde h_a+\widetilde g_a=(D_r)_{aa}=r_a\) for every \(a\).  Therefore a profile with pooled histogram different from \(r\) has no realizing table and has assignment count zero.  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}complete\text{-}randomization}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) then convert these counts to the stated multivariate-hypergeometric probabilities by the common divisor \(\binom{2m}{m}\).

Suppose \(C=(h,g)\sim C'=(h',g')\), and let \(r=h+g\).  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}diagonal\text{-}reduction}\) shows that \(D_r\) is legal, that \(W_{D_r}(C)=Q_r(h)>0\), and that any profile with a different pooled histogram has count zero.  Equality of probabilities in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}probability\text{-}equivalence}\), together with the common positive divisor in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\), therefore forces
\[
 h'+g'=r,
 \qquad
 Q_r(h')=Q_r(h)>0.                                      \tag{1}
\]

Fix distinct \(a,b\in\mathcal A_K\) with \(r_a,r_b>0\), and define
\[
 R^{ab}=D_{r-e_a-e_b}+E_{ab}+E_{ba}.
\]
The diagonal filler is nonnegative, the table has mass \(2m\), and its two off-diagonal effects are \(a-b\) and \(b-a\).  Hence Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}legal\text{-}response\text{-}tables}\) imply \(R^{ab}\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\).

There are four treatment patterns for the two special units.  If both are treated, their pooled observed contribution is \(e_a+e_b\); the same is true if both are controlled.  Either mixed pattern instead contributes \(2e_a\) or \(2e_b\), and so cannot realize a profile whose pooled histogram is \(r\), because the diagonal filler has pooled histogram \(r-e_a-e_b\).  Expanding Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\), with the convention that an out-of-range binomial coefficient is zero, consequently gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_{R^{ab}}(C)
={}&\prod_{c\ne a,b}\binom{r_c}{h_c}
 \left\{
  \binom{r_a-1}{h_a-1}\binom{r_b-1}{h_b-1}
 +\binom{r_a-1}{h_a}\binom{r_b-1}{h_b}
 \right\}\\
={}&Q_r(h)\frac{h_a h_b+g_a g_b}{r_a r_b}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
All divisions are legitimate because \(r_a r_b>0\).  Applying the same calculation to \(C'\), and using (1) and probability equivalence under the legal table \(R^{ab}\), yields
\[
 h_a h_b+g_a g_b=h'_a h'_b+g'_a g'_b.                  \tag{3}
\]

Set \(d=h-g\) and \(d'=h'-g'\).  Since both profiles have pooled histogram \(r\),
\[
 h_a h_b+g_a g_b=\frac{r_a r_b+d_a d_b}{2},
\]
and similarly for the primed profile.  Thus (3) gives
\[
 d_a d_b=d'_a d'_b                                      \tag{4}
\]
for every pair of distinct supported coordinates.  Coordinates outside the support of \(r\) vanish in both vectors.  The equal arm sizes in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}profile\text{-}space}\) give \(\sum_a d_a=\sum_a d'_a=0\); hence, for every \(a\),
\[
 d_a^2=-\sum_{b\ne a}d_a d_b
      =-\sum_{b\ne a}d'_a d'_b=(d'_a)^2.               \tag{5}
\]
If \(d=0\), (5) gives \(d'=0\).  Otherwise choose \(a\) with \(d_a\ne0\).  Equation (5) gives \(d'_a=\varepsilon d_a\) for one \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\), and (4), divided by the nonzero number \(d'_a=\varepsilon d_a\), gives \(d'_b=\varepsilon d_b\) for every \(b\).  Therefore \(d'=d\) or \(d'=-d\).  Since
\[
 h=\frac{r+d}{2},\quad g=\frac{r-d}{2},\quad
 h'=\frac{r+d'}{2},\quad g'=\frac{r-d'}{2},
\]
we obtain \(C'=C\) or \(C'=(g,h)=C^\top\), as asserted.  Notice also that the proof is constructive: failure of a diagonal check is separated by \(D_r\), while, after the diagonal checks pass, failure of (4) is separated by the corresponding two-unit switch \(R^{ab}\).

Choose a labeled schedule having response table \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\).  Suppose an assignment realizes \(C_+\).  If \(S\) is its set of \(m\) treated units, the observed profile says \(a_u=L\) for \(u\in S\) and \(b_u=0\) for \(u\notin S\).  The weak-null equality in Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\) is equality of the two total potential-outcome sums, so
\[
 mL
 \leq mL+\sum_{u\notin S}a_u
 =\sum_{u\in I}a_u
 =\sum_{u\in I}b_u
 =\sum_{u\in S}b_u
 \leq mL.                                                \tag{1}
\]
The endpoint bounds \(0\leq a_u,b_u\leq L\), which follow from the definition of \(\mathcal A_K\), make both inequalities in (1) valid.  Equality throughout forces \(a_u=0\) for every \(u\notin S\) and \(b_u=L\) for every \(u\in S\).  Thus every treated unit has type \((L,L)\), every control unit has type \((0,0)\), and necessarily
\[
 R=mE_{LL}+mE_{00}.                                     \tag{2}
\]
Conversely, for the table in (2), precisely one aggregate assignment chooses all \(m\) units of type \((L,L)\) for treatment, and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) gives \(W_R(C_+)=\binom m m\binom m0=1\).

The same argument with the arms and potential-outcome coordinates interchanged proves that an assignment realizing \(C_-\) is possible only for the table in (2), and there it is the unique assignment treating all \((0,0)\) units.  Therefore \(W_R(C_-)=1\) for (2) and is zero otherwise.  This establishes the two asserted equalities.

We first prove the positive equivalences.  Equality \(C\sim C\) is immediate from Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}probability\text{-}equivalence}\).  If \(K=2\), Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\) reduces to
\[
 R_{10}-R_{01}=0,
\]
so every legal binary response table satisfies \(R=R^\top\).  Complementing a balanced assignment and simultaneously interchanging the two coordinates of every response type gives the coefficient identity
\[
 W_R(h,g)=W_{R^\top}(g,h).                              \tag{1}
\]
This is a bijection because an assignment and its complement both have \(m\) treated units.  Since \(R=R^\top\), (1) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) prove \(C\sim C^\top\) in the binary case.  For every \(K\geq3\), Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}endpoint\text{-}saturation}\) gives equal assignment counts for \(C_+\) and \(C_-\) under every legal table, and hence \(C_+\sim C_-\).

Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}transpose\text{-}reduction}\) proves that no equivalence class can contain anything other than a profile and its transpose.  It remains to decide which nontrivial transpose pairs survive when \(K\geq3\), and to control the number of heterogeneous units in a separator.  Fix \(C=(h,g)\ne C^\top\), put \(r=h+g\), and first suppose that the support
\[
 S=\{a\in\mathcal A_K:r_a>0\}
\]
contains an interior point.  On \(S\), join every distinct pair except possibly \(\{0,L\}\).  This graph is connected because an interior vertex joins both endpoints.  If
\[
 h_a g_b-g_a h_b=0                                      \tag{2}
\]
on every edge, then \(g=r-h\) turns (2) into \(h_a/r_a=h_b/r_b\).  Connectivity makes this ratio constant on \(S\), and the identities \(\sum_a h_a=m\) and \(\sum_a r_a=2m\) make the constant \(1/2\).  That would give \(h=g\), contrary to the choice of \(C\).  Hence there are \(a<b\) with \(\{a,b\}\ne\{0,L\}\) for which (2) is nonzero.

For such \(a,b\), choose \(u,v\in\mathcal A_K\) by
\[
 (u,v)=
 \begin{cases}
 (b-a,0),&a>0,\\
 (b+1,1),&a=0.
 \end{cases}                                             \tag{3}
\]
In the second line \(b<L\), so all four values lie in the alphabet.  In both lines \(a+u=v+b\), and both response types below are heterogeneous.  Define
\[
 R_2=D_{r-e_a-e_b}+E_{av}+E_{ub}.                        \tag{4}
\]
Its mass is \(2m\), its filler is nonnegative because \(r_a,r_b>0\), and the sum of its two nonzero effects is \((a-v)+(u-b)=0\).  Thus (4) is legal by Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\).  Directly checking the two choices in (3) shows that, among the four allocations of the special units, only treating the \((a,v)\) unit and controlling the \((u,b)\) unit adds the pooled histogram \(e_a+e_b\) required on top of the diagonal filler.  Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) therefore gives
\[
 W_{R_2}(C)=Q_r(h)\frac{h_a g_b}{r_a r_b},\qquad
 W_{R_2}(C^\top)=Q_r(h)\frac{g_a h_b}{r_a r_b}.          \tag{5}
\]
The denominator is positive, and (2) says the two counts in (5) differ.  Thus every nontrivial transpose whose pooled histogram has interior support has a legal separator with two heterogeneous units.

It remains to consider profiles supported on \(\{0,L\}\).  Write
\[
 h_0=m-i,\quad h_L=i,\qquad g_0=m-j,\quad g_L=j,\qquad i\ne j. \tag{6}
\]
If only one endpoint were supported, the two arm-size constraints would force \(h=g\), so the relevant pooled endpoint counts are positive.  Consider
\[
 R'_2=D_{r-e_0-e_L}+E_{L,1}+E_{0,L-1}.                  \tag{7}
\]
Here \(L\geq2\).  The two effects in (7) are \(L-1\) and \(-(L-1)\), so the table is legal and has two heterogeneous units.  Because both special control outcomes are interior, an endpoint-only profile is possible only when both special units are treated.  Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_{R'_2}(C)-W_{R'_2}(C^\top)
 &=\frac{Q_r(h)}{r_0r_L}\bigl(h_0h_L-g_0g_L\bigr)\\
 &=\frac{Q_r(h)}{r_0r_L}(i-j)(m-i-j).
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Thus (7) separates unless \(i+j=m\).

Suppose now \(i+j=m\).  Then \(r_0=r_L=m\), \(h_0=j\), \(g_0=i\).  If \(i=0\) or \(j=0\), the unordered pair \(\{C,C^\top\}\) is exactly \(\{C_+,C_-\}\), already shown equivalent.  Otherwise \(i,j>0\); since \(i\ne j\), necessarily \(m\geq3\).  Define the cubic table
\[
 R_3=D_{r-2e_0-e_L}+E_{L,0}+E_{0,1}+E_{0,L-1}.          \tag{9}
\]
Its diagonal filler is nonnegative, and its three heterogeneous effects sum to
\[
 L-1-(L-1)=0,
\]
so (9) is legal.  To produce an endpoint-only profile, the last two special units must be treated, because their control outcomes are interior.  The first special unit must also be treated: if it were controlled, the three special observations would contribute \(3e_0\), rather than the required \(2e_0+e_L\).  Thus exactly one special-unit allocation contributes, even when \(L=2\) and the last two response types coincide.  Binomial cancellation against \(Q_r(h)\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_{R_3}(C)
 &=Q_r(h)\frac{h_0(h_0-1)h_L}{m^2(m-1)},\\
W_{R_3}(C^\top)
 &=Q_r(h)\frac{g_0(g_0-1)g_L}{m^2(m-1)},\\
W_{R_3}(C)-W_{R_3}(C^\top)
 &=Q_r(h)\frac{ij(j-i)}{m^2(m-1)}\ne0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
All divisions in (10) are valid because \(m\geq3\).  Equations (5), (8), and (10), together with Lemmas \(\mathrm{lem{:}transpose\text{-}reduction}\) and \(\mathrm{lem{:}endpoint\text{-}saturation}\), prove the asserted classification for \(K\geq3\).

Finally, the proof supplies the claimed separator map.  If two profiles have different pooled histograms, Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}diagonal\text{-}reduction}\) separates them with \(D_r\), for which \(q=0\).  If their pooled histograms agree but their diagonal coefficients differ, the same diagonal table separates them.  If those checks agree but the profiles are neither equal nor transposes, the constructive proof of Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}transpose\text{-}reduction}\) supplies a symmetric switch with \(q=2\).  A remaining inequivalent transpose at \(K\geq3\) is separated by (4), (7), or (9), with \(q=2,2,3\), respectively.  Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separator\text{-}size}\) therefore gives \(d(C,C')\leq3\) for every inequivalent pair.

Put \(j=m-i\).  The stated profiles have endpoint coordinates
\[
 h_0=j,\quad h_L=i,\qquad g_0=i,\quad g_L=j,            \tag{1}
\]
and zero interior coordinates.  Since \(1\leq i,j\leq m-1\), they are not the endpoint corners; since \(2i\ne m\), they are distinct transposes.  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) therefore makes them inequivalent and gives \(d(C,C')\leq3\).  We prove the reverse inequality.

Fix any \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) with \(q(R)\leq2\).  If \(q(R)=0\), the table is diagonal.  If its diagonal histogram is not \(m e_0+m e_L\), both profiles in (1) have zero count; if it is that histogram, Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) and binomial symmetry give
\[
 W_R(C)=\binom mj\binom mi=W_R(C').                     \tag{2}
\]
The case \(q(R)=1\) is impossible: all diagonal units have zero effect, while the sole heterogeneous unit would have a nonzero effect, contradicting Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\).

It remains to treat \(q(R)=2\).  Label the two heterogeneous units \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\).  The weak null says
\[
 a+c=b+d.                                                \tag{3}
\]
If a diagonal filler unit has an interior outcome, both endpoint-only profiles have count zero.  We may therefore suppose that every diagonal filler unit is at \(0\) or \(L\).  Expand the assignment count according to which of the two special units are treated.  If an observed special outcome is interior, its contribution is zero for both profiles.  For the remaining possibilities we compare the contributions term by term.

If both special units are treated, their observed outcomes are \(a,c\in\{0,L\}\).  They cannot both be zero, because (3) and nonnegativity would force \(b=d=0\), making both units diagonal.  They cannot both be \(L\), because (3) and the upper bound \(b,d\leq L\) would force \(b=d=L\).  Thus their observed multiset is \(\{0,L\}\).  A nonzero contribution then requires \(m-1\) diagonal fillers at each endpoint, and the two profile coefficients are
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j-1}\binom{m-1}{i-1}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i-1}\binom{m-1}{j-1},                     \tag{4}
\]
which agree.  If both special units are controlled, the identical argument applied to \(b,d\) gives the equal coefficients
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j}\binom{m-1}{i}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i}\binom{m-1}{j}.                         \tag{5}
\]

Finally suppose exactly one special unit is treated.  For definiteness, let the observed outcomes be \(a\) from the first unit and \(d\) from the second.  If \(a,d\in\{0,L\}\) are different, then (3) forces the unobserved outcomes to be the same respective endpoints: for \((a,d)=(0,L)\), one has \(c-b=L\), hence \((c,b)=(L,0)\), and both response types are diagonal; the reverse case is symmetric.  This contradicts their designation as heterogeneous.  Therefore the two observed outcomes equal some \(v\in\{0,L\}\).  Equation (3) then gives \(b=c\), so the special response types have the form \((v,u)\) and \((u,v)\) with \(u\ne v\).  One observation of \(v\) lies in each arm.  A nonzero contribution requires \(m-2\) diagonal fillers at \(v\) and \(m\) at the other endpoint \(\bar v=L-v\).  Its coefficients for \(C\) and \(C'\) are
\[
 \binom{m-2}{h_v-1}\binom m{h_{\bar v}}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \binom{m-2}{g_v-1}\binom m{g_{\bar v}}.              \tag{6}
\]
They agree because (1) gives \(h_v+g_v=m\) and \(h_{\bar v}+g_{\bar v}=m\), so each binomial coefficient in (6) equals its complementary coefficient.  The other split allocation is identical with the two labels exchanged.

The four allocations of the special units exhaust Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\).  Equations (4)--(6) therefore imply \(W_R(C)=W_R(C')\) for every legal \(R\) with \(q(R)\leq2\).  Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) gives the same equality for probabilities, so Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separator\text{-}size}\) yields \(d(C,C')\geq3\).  Together with the upper bound, this proves \(d(C,C')=3\).

For the requested smallest-instance audit, take \(K=3\), \(m=3\), \(L=2\), and \(i=1\).  Formula (9) in the proof of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) becomes
\[
 R=E_{20}+2E_{01}+E_{00}+2E_{22}.
\]
Both potential-outcome totals are \(6\), and direct expansion over its \(\binom63=20\) balanced assignments gives counts \(1\) for \(C=((2,0,1),(1,0,2))\) and \(0\) for \(C'\).  Independently enumerating the nonnegative \(3\times3\) integer tables of mass \(6\), imposing the weak-null equation and \(q(R)\leq2\), leaves \(103\) tables; the exhaustive allocation argument above gives equal counts for every one of them.  Thus the cubic witness passes the finite early-kill check without the check being used as a premise of the general proof.

For a bijection \(f\) of \(\mathcal X_{m,K}\), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}maximal\text{-}common\text{-}group}\) says
\[
 f\in G_\star
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 P_R(f(C))=P_R(C)\ \text{for every }C\in\mathcal X_{m,K}
 \text{ and }R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K).
\]
By Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}probability\text{-}equivalence}\), the right-hand side is exactly the assertion that \(f(C)\) belongs to the \(\sim\)-class of \(C\) for every \(C\).  Since the profile space is finite and \(f\) is bijective, this is equivalent to saying that \(f\) restricts to an arbitrary permutation of each equivalence class.  Conversely, every collection of within-class permutations preserves every \(P_R\) by the definition of the classes.  Composition and inversion act coordinatewise, so
\[
 G_\star\cong\prod_{A\in\mathcal X_{m,K}/\sim} S_A.     \tag{1}
\]

When \(K=2\), a histogram of arm size \(m\) is determined by its count of outcome \(1\), so \(|\mathcal X_{m,2}|=(m+1)^2\).  Exactly \(m+1\) profiles satisfy \(C=C^\top\).  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) says that every other class is a two-point transpose class, whose number is
\[
 \frac{(m+1)^2-(m+1)}2=\frac{m(m+1)}2=\binom{m+1}{2}.   \tag{2}
\]
The singleton factors in (1) are trivial, and (2) yields
\(G_\star\cong(S_2)^{\binom{m+1}{2}}\).  When \(K\geq3\), the same theorem gives one two-point class \(\{C_+,C_-\}\) and only singleton classes otherwise.  Equation (1) then gives \(G_\star\cong S_2\), with its sole nontrivial action exchanging the two corners.

Fix \(G\leq G_\star\), a statistic \(T\), and a profile \(C\).  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}maximal\text{-}common\text{-}group}\) shows that every \(G\)-orbit has one or two points.  If the orbit of \(C\) is a singleton, every \(f\in G\) fixes \(C\), and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}orbit\text{-}rank\text{-}pvalue}\) gives \(p_G(C)=1\).  If its orbit is \(\{C,C^*\}\), the orbit--stabilizer counting bijection gives exactly \(|G|/2\) elements sending \(C\) to each of \(C\) and \(C^*\).  Because \(T(C)\geq T(C)\),
\[
 p_G(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  1/2,&T(C^*)<T(C),\\
  1,&T(C^*)\geq T(C).
 \end{cases}                                             \tag{1}
\]
Thus \(p_G(C)\in\{1/2,1\}\) for every profile, including for the trivial subgroup.

Now fix a legal response table \(R\).  By the defining property of \(G_\star\),
\[
 P_R(f(C))=P_R(C)\qquad(f\in G).                         \tag{2}
\]
Consequently the random profile is uniform conditional on each positive-probability \(G\)-orbit: (2) assigns the same mass to every point of that orbit.  If \(0\leq\alpha<1/2\), (1) makes the rejection event empty.  If \(1/2\leq\alpha<1\), a singleton orbit contributes no rejection, and a two-point orbit contributes at most one of its two equally likely points, because both points cannot strictly exceed one another under \(T\).  Therefore, summing over the disjoint orbits,
\[
 \Pr_R\{p_G(C)\leq\alpha\}\leq\frac12\leq\alpha.     \tag{3}
\]
For \(\alpha=1\), the probability is \(1\).  Equations (1)--(3) prove both the granularity and the finite-sample validity claimed in the theorem, using only the balanced design probability kernel in Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}complete\text{-}randomization}\).

Let \(B=\binom{2m}{m}\), which is positive because \(m\geq1\).  By Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}corner\text{-}pvalue}\), if \(0\leq\alpha<B^{-1}\), the event \(\{p_{\mathrm{corner}}(C)\leq\alpha\}\) is empty.  If \(B^{-1}\leq\alpha<1\), that event is exactly \(\{C=C_+\}\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}endpoint\text{-}saturation}\), Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}complete\text{-}randomization}\), and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) give
\[
 \Pr_R(C=C_+)=P_R(C_+)=\frac{W_R(C_+)}B\in\{0,B^{-1}\}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 \Pr_R\{p_{\mathrm{corner}}(C)\leq\alpha\}
 \leq B^{-1}\leq\alpha.
\]
For \(\alpha=1\), the event is the whole profile space and its probability is \(1\).  These cases exhaust \([0,1]\) and establish exact validity for every legal \(R\).  The only value below one is \(B^{-1}\).  It equals \(1/2\) when \(m=1\) and is strictly smaller than \(1/2\) whenever \(m\geq2\), since then \(B=\binom{2m}{m}\geq6\).  Hence the nontrivial value can indeed be strictly below \(1/2\), without making any claim about the granularity of other exact tests.

theorem.statement:
Let \(n=2m\), \(K\geq 2\), \(1\leq n_1,n_0\leq n-1\), \(n_1+n_0=n\), and \(n_1\neq n_0\). Under complete randomization, the treated set is uniform over the \(\binom n{n_1}\) subsets of size \(n_1\), while the potential-outcome response table \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\), and hence the causal weak-null condition \(\tau_R=0\), is fixed. Complete the rectangular coefficient handle \(\mathsf H_{\mathrm{unbal}}\) by putting
\[
 \mathcal X_{n_1,n_0,K}
 =\left\{(h,g)\in\mathbb Z_+^K\times\mathbb Z_+^K:
       \sum_a h_a=n_1,\ \sum_a g_a=n_0\right\},
\]
\[
 \mathcal T_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)
 =\left\{T\in\mathbb Z_+^{K\times K}:0\leq T_{ab}\leq R_{ab},\quad
       \sum_bT_{ab}=h_a,\quad \sum_a(R_{ab}-T_{ab})=g_b\right\},
\]
and
\[
 W_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)}
       \prod_{a,b\in\mathcal A_K}\binom{R_{ab}}{T_{ab}},
 \qquad
 P_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)=\binom n{n_1}^{-1}W_R^{(n_1)}(h,g).
\]
For \(C,C'\in\mathcal X_{n_1,n_0,K}\), define \(C\sim_{n_1,n_0}C'\) when \(P_R^{(n_1)}(C)=P_R^{(n_1)}(C')\) for every \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\). Then
\[
 C\sim_{n_1,n_0}C'\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C=C'.
\]
Consequently the maximal common bijection group
\[
 G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}
 =\left\{f\in\operatorname{Bij}(\mathcal X_{n_1,n_0,K}):
 P_R^{(n_1)}(f(C))=P_R^{(n_1)}(C)\ \text{for every }C,R\right\}
\]
is \(\{\operatorname{id}\}\). Moreover, if
\[
 s_\star(n_1,n_0,K)
 =\max_{C\neq C'}\ \min\left\{q(R):R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K),\quad
       P_R^{(n_1)}(C)\neq P_R^{(n_1)}(C')\right\},
\]
then
\[
 s_\star(n_1,n_0,K)=2.
\]
Thus two heterogeneous units always suffice, by an explicit legal response table, and this uniform bound cannot be reduced.
theorem.proof_tex:
Write \(C=(h,g)\), \(C'=(h',g')\), and adopt the convention \(\binom uv=0\) unless \(0\leq v\leq u\). The displayed coefficient formula is first verified from the design. For a fixed response table \(R\), a treated-count matrix \(T\) specifies that exactly \(T_{ab}\) of the \(R_{ab}\) labeled units of type \((a,b)\) are treated. There are
\[
 \prod_{a,b\in\mathcal A_K}\binom{R_{ab}}{T_{ab}}
\]
such assignments. The row constraints on \(T\) give the treated histogram \(h\), and the column constraints on \(R-T\) give the control histogram \(g\). Distinct matrices \(T\) describe disjoint assignments, so summation gives \(W_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)\). Since the complete-randomization design assigns probability \(\binom n{n_1}^{-1}\) to each assignment, division by the positive number \(\binom n{n_1}\) gives \(P_R^{(n_1)}\).

For a vector \(r\in\mathbb Z_+^K\) with \(\sum_a r_a=n\), let \(D(r)\) be the diagonal table with \(D(r)_{aa}=r_a\). Its mass is \(n\), and every unit has effect zero; hence both the finite-table normalization and the weak-null condition hold, so \(D(r)\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\). Directly from the preceding count,
\[
 W_{D(r)}^{(n_1)}(u,v)
 =\mathbf 1\{u+v=r\}\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\binom{r_a}{u_a}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Set \(r=h+g\) and
\[
 Q_r(h)=\prod_a\binom{r_a}{h_a}.
\]
Every factor in \(Q_r(h)\) is positive because \(0\leq h_a\leq r_a\). If \(C\sim_{n_1,n_0}C'\), applying (1) to \(D(r)\) shows first that \(h'+g'=r\), since the count of \(C\) is positive, and then that
\[
 Q_r(h)=Q_r(h').
 \tag{2}
\]

We next extract all quadratic information by legal two-unit switches. Let \(e_a\) denote the coordinate vector at level \(a\), and let \(E_{ab}\) denote the response table of one unit of type \((a,b)\). If \(a\neq b\) and \(r_a,r_b>0\), define
\[
 R^{ab}=D(r-e_a-e_b)+E_{ab}+E_{ba}.
 \tag{3}
\]
The table in (3) has mass \(n\), while the effects of its two heterogeneous units sum to \((a-b)+(b-a)=0\). Thus it is legal and \(q(R^{ab})=2\). The two special units contribute pooled observed outcomes \(e_a+e_b\) when both are treated or both are controlled, \(2e_a\) when the \((a,b)\) unit alone is treated, and \(2e_b\) in the opposite mixed allocation. Because the diagonal filler in (3) has pooled histogram \(r-e_a-e_b\), only the first two allocations can realize a profile whose pooled histogram is \(r\). Applying the elementary identities
\[
 \binom{s-1}{t-1}=\frac ts\binom st,
 \qquad
 \binom{s-1}{t}=\frac{s-t}{s}\binom st
\]
with the strictly positive denominators \(s=r_a,r_b\) gives
\[
 W_{R^{ab}}^{(n_1)}(h,g)
 =Q_r(h)\frac{h_ah_b+g_ag_b}{r_ar_b}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Define the arm-imbalance vectors
\[
 d=h-g=2h-r,\qquad d'=h'-g'=2h'-r.
\]
Since
\[
 h_ah_b+g_ag_b=\frac{r_ar_b+d_ad_b}{2},
 \tag{5}
\]
equivalence, (2), and (4) imply
\[
 d_ad_b=d'_ad'_b
 \quad\text{for all distinct }a,b\text{ with }r_a,r_b>0.
 \tag{6}
\]

The diagonal entries of the same outer product are obtained from a second placement of the switch. Fix \(a\) with \(r_a\geq2\), choose any \(b\neq a\), which is possible because \(K\geq2\), and put
\[
 \widetilde R^{a\mid b}=D(r-2e_a)+E_{ab}+E_{ba}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Again the mass is \(n\), the two nonzero effects cancel, and \(q(\widetilde R^{a\mid b})=2\). The filler in (7) has pooled histogram \(r-2e_a\). Exactly one allocation of the special units supplies the missing pooled histogram \(2e_a\): the \((a,b)\) unit is treated and the \((b,a)\) unit is controlled. The other three allocations supply \(e_a+e_b\) or \(2e_b\), which differ because \(a\neq b\). Therefore
\[
 W_{\widetilde R^{a\mid b}}^{(n_1)}(h,g)
 =\prod_c\binom{r_c-2\mathbf 1\{c=a\}}
                       {h_c-\mathbf 1\{c=a\}}
 =Q_r(h)\frac{h_ag_a}{r_a(r_a-1)}.
 \tag{8}
\]
All divisions in (8) are valid because \(r_a\geq2\). Equivalence and (2) now imply \(h_ag_a=h'_ag'_a\), and hence
\[
 d_a^2=r_a^2-4h_ag_a=r_a^2-4h'_ag'_a=(d'_a)^2.
 \tag{9}
\]
If \(r_a=0\), both corresponding imbalance coordinates vanish. If \(r_a=1\), integrality and \(h_a,h'_a\in\{0,1\}\) give \(d_a^2=(d'_a)^2=1\). Thus (9) holds for every \(a\); together with (6), including the trivial products involving a zero-support coordinate, it yields
\[
 dd^{\mathsf T}=d'(d')^{\mathsf T}.
 \tag{10}
\]

The unequal allocation is used precisely now. Both profile constraints give
\[
 \sum_a d_a=\sum_a d'_a=n_1-n_0=:\delta\neq0.
 \tag{11}
\]
In particular \(d\neq0\). Choose \(j\) with \(d_j\neq0\). By (10), \(d'_j=\varepsilon d_j\) for some \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\), and the \((j,a)\) entries of (10) give \(d'_a=\varepsilon d_a\) for every \(a\). Summing and using (11) gives \(\delta=\varepsilon\delta\); positivity of \(|\delta|\) forces \(\varepsilon=1\). Hence \(d'=d\), and then
\[
 h'=\frac{r+d'}2=\frac{r+d}2=h,
 \qquad
 g'=\frac{r-d'}2=\frac{r-d}2=g.
\]
This proves that every equivalence class is a singleton.

The argument is constructive for every distinct pair. If the pooled histograms differ, (1) with \(D(h+g)\) separates them. If their pooled histograms agree but their values of \(Q_r\) differ, the same diagonal table separates them. Otherwise (2) holds. If some off-diagonal product in (6) differs, the table (3) separates the pair by (4). If no such product differs, distinctness and the implication (10)--(11) show that some squared coordinate must differ. Such a coordinate necessarily has \(r_a\geq2\), and (7) separates the pair by (8). Every displayed separator is legal and has \(q\leq2\). It follows immediately from the singleton partition that a common probability-preserving bijection fixes every profile, so \(G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}=\{\operatorname{id}\}\), and the preceding construction proves
\[
 s_\star(n_1,n_0,K)\leq2.
 \tag{12}
\]

It remains to certify sharpness uniformly over all admissible \((n_1,n_0,K)\). Since \(n=2m\) and \(n_1\neq n_0\), one has \(m\geq2\). Define
\[
 \ell=\max\{0,n_1-m\},\qquad u=\min\{m,n_1\}.
\]
The bounds \(1\leq n_1\leq2m-1\) give \(\ell<u\), and a direct split into \(n_1\leq m\) and \(n_1>m\) gives \(\ell+u=n_1\). Using levels \(0,1\in\mathcal A_K\), define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 h&=\ell e_0+u e_1,
 &g&=(m-\ell)e_0+(m-u)e_1,\\
 h'&=u e_0+\ell e_1,
 &g'&=(m-u)e_0+(m-\ell)e_1.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{13}
\]
Both profiles have arm sizes \((n_1,n_0)\), both have pooled histogram \(r=me_0+me_1\), and they are distinct because \(\ell<u\). If a legal table has \(q(R)=0\), then it is diagonal. Formula (1) makes both counts zero unless \(R=D(r)\), while for \(R=D(r)\),
\[
 W_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)=\binom m\ell\binom mu
 =\binom mu\binom m\ell
 =W_R^{(n_1)}(h',g').
 \tag{14}
\]
There is no legal table with \(q(R)=1\): all diagonal units have zero effect, whereas the single heterogeneous unit would contribute the nonzero effect \(a-b\), contradicting the weak-null sum. Thus the pair (13) cannot be separated with fewer than two heterogeneous units. Combining this fact with (12) proves
\[
 s_\star(n_1,n_0,K)=2.
\]

For the smallest admissible instance \((n,K,n_1,n_0)=(4,2,1,3)\), (13) gives the two profiles \((h,g)=((0,1),(2,1))\) and \((h',g')=((1,0),(1,2))\). Their diagonal counts under \(D(2e_0+2e_1)\) are both \(2\), and all other diagonal tables give both count zero. The legal table \(2E_{11}+E_{01}+E_{10}\), which is (7) with \(a=0,b=1\), gives assignment counts \(0\) and \(1\), respectively, by (8). This exact enumeration checks both the upper construction and the lower obstruction at the boundary case.
